speak.prosody: Chapter 5 The Power of Financial Education—Why Schools Don’t Teach Money Skills It’s interesting, isn’t it? We spend years in school learning algebra, history, and science, but the subject of money is rarely, if ever, discussed. Most people graduate knowing how to solve equations, but not how to manage a budget, invest in the stock market, or start their own business. Because of this, many of us step into adulthood completely unprepared for the financial realities we’re about to face. The boy experienced this difference up close. His father, who was highly educated with years of schooling and advanced degrees, still struggled with money. He knew how to earn a paycheck, but he didn’t understand how to make money work for him. Meanwhile, his friend’s father, who hadn’t gone as far in formal education, somehow seemed to have figured out the secret to building wealth. This contrast brought up a big question: why don’t schools teach us about money? The answer comes down to tradition. Our education system was designed for a different time—a time when steady jobs and reliable pensions were the norm. But times have changed. Job security isn’t a given anymore, and people who depend only on a paycheck often find themselves vulnerable to layoffs, changing economies, and surprise expenses. The friend’s father was convinced that understanding how money works was the most important skill anyone could have. He encouraged the boys to read books, go to seminars, and seek out mentors. He always reminded them that financial education isn’t something you learn once and forget—it’s a lifelong journey. The world of money is always changing, and if you stop learning, you quickly fall behind. He also made it clear that learning isn’t enough on its own. Knowing about investing or entrepreneurship is one thing, but real understanding comes from action. That means buying your first stock, starting a small business, or negotiating a deal. You’re bound to make mistakes along the way, but each mistake is a lesson you can’t find in any textbook. As time went on, the boy realized that financial education goes way beyond just numbers. It’s really about your mindset, your daily habits, and your willingness to keep learning. People who take charge of their own financial education start to see opportunities where others only see roadblocks. They become more resilient, more adaptable, and able to build a life that’s not limited by fear or the usual expectations.
